title: Pretraining and transfer: BERT 2018, GPT-2 2019, GPT-3 2020
story:
Before this shift, a model for a task was trained on data labelled for that task, and it learned two things at once: how the language works, and what you wanted done with it. The second is the part you cared about. The first is most of the work, and it was paid for again from scratch on every new task, which meant a task with no labelled corpus behind it was simply not attempted.

Pretraining splits those apart. Learn the language once, from text nobody had to label, and attach the task afterwards. That sentence is the whole idea, and everything since is an argument about how small the attaching step can get.

The 2018 work of Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova is the clean statement of the first form. It pre-trains deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers, so that the pre-trained model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer for a wide range of tasks, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. It reported new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks and pushed the GLUE score to 80.5, an absolute improvement of 7.7.

Read the second half of that sentence rather than the first. Eleven results are a headline; one additional output layer without substantial architecture modifications is the change. Previously each task got its own architecture, designed by someone who knew that task. Afterwards the architecture is the same one every time and the task is a thin layer on top, which means progress on the shared part is progress on all of them at once.

Then the attaching step gets smaller. The 2019 report from Radford and colleagues describes a model of 1.5 billion parameters trained on a corpus built from millions of web pages, reaching state-of-the-art results on seven of eight tested language modelling datasets in a zero-shot setting while still underfitting that corpus — and it argues that model capacity is essential to zero-shot task transfer, with performance improving log-linearly across tasks as capacity grows. No fine-tuning at all for those results. The task was communicated in the input.

And in 2020 Brown, Mann, Ryder and colleagues took it to an autoregressive model of 175 billion parameters, ten times more than any previous non-sparse language model, applied to all tasks without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model.

That last clause is the one to hold on to, because it is the moment the interface changed. Using a model stopped being an engineering task with a training loop and became an act of description. Everyone who writes a prompt today is doing what that paper introduced, and the reason prompting is a skill at all is that specifying a task in text is genuinely harder than it looks, not that the model is fragile.

Now the correction that comes with it, which is small and matters. The 2020 paper points out that its predecessor described its own results as zero-shot task transfer while sometimes providing task examples in context, which is better described as one-shot or few-shot transfer. The field had been slightly misdescribing what it was doing, and noticed afterwards. That is worth remembering when a term is being used loudly.

Be careful with the word learning in few-shot learning, for the same reason. There are no gradient updates. The weights are identical before and after your examples, and nothing has been retained — the demonstrations change the prediction because they are part of the input, the way a worked example at the top of a page changes what a reader writes next. Say learning and you have implied the model now knows something, so people ask why it forgot by the next session. It did not forget. It was never told.

What you actually inherit is worth stating plainly, since it is the cost of the whole arrangement. The expensive half of the model is no longer something you built, it is something you were given. What it knows, what it absorbed, and what it will reproduce are questions about a corpus you did not see and cannot audit — and the 2020 paper flags methodological issues related to training on large web corpora itself. The move that made every task cheap also made the foundation of every task someone else's work, and that is the trade you are making when you start from a pretrained model, which is to say almost always.

problem.name: Pretraining and transfer
problem.shape: Every task needs the same general competence, and only a little that is specific to it.
tell: the labelled data for this task is small or does not exist
several tasks in the system need the same underlying competence
a task-specific architecture is being designed before anything has been tried
someone describes examples in a prompt as the model learning
problem.move: Take the general competence from a model trained on unlabelled text and add only what is specific to your task — a thin fine-tuned layer, or just a description and a few demonstrations in the input. Then be explicit about which of those you did, because only one of them changes the weights.
problem.invariant: Demonstrations in the input change the output without changing the model: there are no gradient updates, so the weights are identical before and after and nothing is retained between calls.
problem.breaks: The expensive half is inherited, so what the model knows, what it absorbed and what it will reproduce are properties of a corpus you did not see and cannot audit.

cost.time: the general training is paid once by somebody else; your per-task cost is a small fine-tune or nothing at all
cost.space: demonstrations live in the input, so every call pays for them again in context and in latency
cost.beats: training a task-specific model from scratch, which needs a labelled corpus per task and re-learns the language every time

worked.problem: What did pretraining separate, and why is a demonstration in the prompt not the model learning?
worked.reasoning:
It separated learning the language from learning the task.

Before, both happened at once, from data labelled for the task in hand. That meant the general part — how the language works — was re-learned from scratch for every task, and paid for with labelled data each time, so a task without a labelled corpus behind it was out of reach.

Pretraining does the general part once, on text nobody labelled, and attaches the task afterwards. The 2018 work is the clearest version of the first form: pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text, then fine-tune with just one additional output layer for a wide range of tasks, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. It reported state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks.

The part I would emphasise is not the eleven results but the one additional output layer. Task-specific architecture stopped being where the work went, so improvements to the shared foundation lifted every task at once.

Then the attaching step shrank twice. In 2019 a model of 1.5 billion parameters reached state of the art on seven of eight language modelling datasets with no fine-tuning at all, arguing that capacity is essential to zero-shot task transfer and that performance improves log-linearly as capacity grows. In 2020 a model of 175 billion parameters was applied to all tasks without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with the task and its demonstrations specified purely via text interaction.

On why a demonstration in the prompt is not learning: there are no gradient updates. The weights are the same before and after, and nothing is retained. The examples change the output because they are part of the input, the way a worked example at the top of a page changes what a reader writes next — not because the model absorbed them.

The distinction is practical and not pedantic. Say the model learned from the examples and you have implied it knows something now, which leads people to expect it in the next session, to wonder why it forgot, and to plan around a memory that does not exist. It did not forget. It was never told.

I would also mention that the field corrected its own vocabulary here: the 2020 paper notes its predecessor called results zero-shot while sometimes providing examples in context, which is better described as one-shot or few-shot. A term everybody is repeating is worth checking against what was actually done.

And the cost, since it is the trade every project now makes: the expensive half of the model is inherited rather than built, so what it knows and what it absorbed are questions about a corpus you did not see and cannot audit — something the 2020 paper flags about large web corpora itself.

problem.practice: Give a model a fact it cannot know, in the prompt, and let it use the fact correctly. Then start a new session and ask about the same fact. Watching it fail the second time is the clearest demonstration that nothing was learned, and it will stop you designing around a memory that does not exist.

beats.broke: A model trained per task learned the language and the task together from labelled data, so every task paid for the general half again and tasks without a labelled corpus were not attempted.
beats.fix: Learn the language once from unlabelled text and attach the task afterwards — first as one extra fine-tuned layer, then as nothing but a description and demonstrations in the input.
beats.cost: The expensive half is inherited rather than built, so what the model knows is a property of a corpus you did not see and cannot audit.

interview.q: What did pretraining separate, and why is a demonstration in the prompt not the model learning?
interview.trap: Calling in-context demonstrations learning. It implies the model now knows something, which leads people to expect it in the next session and to design around a memory that does not exist.
interview.answer:

On the second half of the question: there are no gradient updates. The weights are identical before and after, nothing is retained, and the demonstrations change the output only because they are part of the input — like a worked example at the top of a page.

takeaway: Pretraining separated learning the language from learning the task, and the attaching step shrank from one fine-tuned output layer to a description written in the input — but demonstrations in a prompt involve no gradient updates, so nothing is learned and nothing is retained, and the half you inherited came from a corpus you cannot audit.
